jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.intro.text:
THE NATURE AND USE OF PROVERBS.--A proverb is a pithy sentence, concisely expressing some well-established truth susceptible of various illustrations and applications. The word is of Latin derivation, literally meaning for a word, speech, or discourse; that is, one expression for many. The Hebrew word for "proverb" (mashal) means a "comparison." Many suppose it was used, because the form or matter of the proverb, or both, involved the idea of comparison. Most of the proverbs are in couplets or triplets, or some modifications of them, the members of which correspond in structure and length, as if arranged to be compared one with another. They illustrate the varieties of parallelism, a distinguishing feature of Hebrew poetry. Compare Introduction to Poetical Books. Many also clearly involve the idea of comparison in the sentiments expressed (compare Pro 12:1-10; Pro 25:10-15; Pro 26:1-9). Sometimes, however, the designed omission of one member of the comparison, exercising the reader's sagacity or study for its supply, presents the proverb as a "riddle" or "dark saying" (compare Pro. 30:15-33; Pro 1:6; Psa 49:4). The sententious form of expression, which thus became a marked feature of the proverbial style, was also adopted for continuous discourse, even when not always preserving traces of comparison, either in form or matter (compare Pro. 1:1-9:18). In Eze 17:1; Eze 24:3, we find the same word properly translated "parable," to designate an illustrative discourse. Then the Greek translators have used a word, parabola ("parable"), which the gospel writers (except John) employ for our Lord's discourses of the same character, and which also seems to involve the idea of comparison, though that may not be its primary meaning. It might seem, therefore, that the proverbial and parabolic styles of writing were originally and essentially the same. The proverb is a "concentrated parable, and the parable an extension of the proverb by a full illustration." The proverb is thus the moral or theme of a parable, which sometimes precedes it, as in Mat 19:30 (compare Pro 20:1); or succeeds it, as in Mat. 22:1-16; Luk 15:1-10. The style being poetical, and adapted to the expression of a high order of poetical sentiment, such as prophecy, we find the same term used to designate such compositions (compare Num 23:7; Mic 2:4; Hab 2:6).

Though the Hebrews used the same term for proverb and parable, the Greek employs two, though the sacred writers have not always appeared to recognize a distinction. The term for proverb is, paroimia, which the Greek translators employ for the title of this book, evidently with special reference to the later definition of a proverb, as a trite, sententious form of speech, which appears to be the best meaning of the term. John uses the same term to designate our Saviour's instructions, in view of their characteristic obscurity (compare Pro 16:25-29, Greek), and even for his illustrative discourses (Pro 10:6), whose sense was not at once obvious to all his hearers. This form of instruction was well adapted to aid the learner. The parallel structure of sentences, the repetition, contrast, or comparison of thought, were all calculated to facilitate the efforts of memory; and precepts of practical wisdom which, extended into logical discourses, might have failed to make abiding impressions by reason of their length or complicated character, were thus compressed into pithy, and, for the most part, very plain statements. Such a mode of instruction has distinguished the written or traditional literature of all nations, and was, and still is, peculiarly current in the East.

In this book, however, we are supplied with a proverbial wisdom commended by the seal of divine inspiration. God has condescended to become our teacher on the practical affairs belonging to all the relations of life. He has adapted His instruction to the plain and unlettered, and presented, in this striking and impressive method, the great principles of duty to Him and to our fellow men. To the prime motive of all right conduct, the fear of God, are added all lawful and subordinate incentives, such as honor, interest, love, fear, and natural affection. Besides the terror excited by an apprehension of God's justly provoked judgments, we are warned against evil-doing by the exhibition of the inevitable temporal results of impiety, injustice, profligacy, idleness, laziness, indolence, drunkenness, and debauchery. To the rewards of true piety which follow in eternity, are promised the peace, security, love, and approbation of the good, and the comforts of a clear conscience, which render this life truly happy.

INSPIRATION AND AUTHORSHIP.--With no important exception, Jewish and Christian writers have received this book as the inspired production of Solomon. It is the first book of the Bible prefaced by the name of the author. The New Testament abounds with citations from the Proverbs. Its intrinsic excellence commends it to us as the production of a higher authority than the apocryphal writings, such as Wisdom or Ecclesiasticus. Solomon lived five hundred years before the "seven wise men" of Greece, and seven hundred before the age of Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle. It is thus very evident, whatever theory of his sources of knowledge be adopted, that he did not draw upon any heathen repositories with which we are acquainted. It is far more probable, that by the various migrations, captivities, and dispersions of the Jews, heathen philosophers drew from this inspired fountain many of those streams which continue to refresh mankind amid the otherwise barren and parched deserts of profane literature.

As, however, the Psalms are ascribed to David, because he was the leading author, so the ascription of this book to Solomon is entirely consistent with the titles of the thirtieth and thirty-first chapters, which assign those chapters to Agur and Lemuel respectively. Of these persons we know nothing. This is not the place for discussing the various speculations respecting them. By a slight change of reading some propose to translate Pro 30:1 : "The words of Agur, the son of her who was obeyed Massa," that is, "the queen of Massa"; and Pro 31:1 : "The words of Lemuel, king of Massa"; but to this the earliest versions are contradictory, and nothing other than the strongest exegetical necessity ought to be allowed to justify a departure from a well-established reading and version when nothing useful to our knowledge is gained. It is better to confess ignorance than indulge in useless conjectures.

It is probable that out of the "three thousand proverbs" (Kg1 4:32) which Solomon spoke, he selected and edited Pro. 1:1-24:34 during his life. Pro. 25:1-29:27 were also of his production, and copied out in the days of Hezekiah, by his "men," perhaps the prophets Isaiah, Hosea, and Micah. Such a work was evidently in the spirit of this pious monarch, who set his heart so fully on a reformation of God's worship. Learned men have endeavored to establish the theory that Solomon himself was only a collector; or that the other parts of the book, as these chapters, were also selections by later hands; but the reasons adduced to maintain these views have never appeared so satisfactory as to change the usual opinions on the subject, which have the sanction of the most ancient and reliable authorities.

DIVISIONS OF THE BOOK.--Such a work is, of course, not susceptible of any logical analysis. There are, however, some well-defined marks of division, so that very generally the book is divided into five or six parts.

1. The first contains nine chapters, in which are discussed and enforced by illustration, admonition, and encouragement the principles and blessings of wisdom, and the pernicious schemes and practices of sinful persons. These chapters are introductory. With few specimens of the proper proverb, they are distinguished by its conciseness and terseness. The sentences follow very strictly the form of parallelism, and generally of the synonymous species, only forty of the synthetic and four (Pro 3:32-35) of the antithetic appearing. The style is ornate, the figures bolder and fuller, and the illustrations more striking and extended.

2. The antithetic and synthetic parallelism to the exclusion of the synonymous distinguish Pro. 10:1-22:16, and the verses are entirely unconnected, each containing a complete sense in itself.

3. Pro. 22:16-24:34 present a series of admonitions as if addressed to a pupil, and generally each topic occupies two or more verses.

4. Pro. 25:1-29:27 are entitled to be regarded as a distinct portion, for the reason given above as to its origin. The style is very much mixed; of the peculiarities, compare parts two and three.

5. Pro. 30:1-33 is peculiar not only for its authorship, but as a specimen of the kind of proverb which has been described as "dark sayings" or "riddles."

6. To a few pregnant but concise admonitions, suitable for a king, is added a most inimitable portraiture of female character. In both parts five and six the distinctive peculiarity of the original proverbial style gives place to the modifications already mentioned as marking a later composition, though both retain the concise and nervous method of stating truth, equally valuable for its deep impression and permanent retention by the memory.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.1.intro.text: After the title the writer defines the design and nature of the instructions of the book. He paternally invites attention to those instructions and warns his readers against the enticements of the wicked. In a beautiful personification, wisdom is then introduced in a most solemn and impressive manner, publicly inviting men to receive its teachings, warning those who reject, and encouraging those who accept, the proffered instructions. (Pro. 1:1-33)

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.1.20.text:
Some interpreters regard this address as the language of the Son of God under the name of Wisdom (compare Luk 11:49). Others think that wisdom, as the divine attribute specially employed in acts of counsel and admonition, is here personified, and represents God. In either case the address is a most solemn and divine admonition, whose matter and spirit are eminently evangelical and impressive (see on Pro 8:1). 

Wisdom--literally, "Wisdoms," the plural used either because of the unusual sense, or as indicative of the great excellency of wisdom (compare Pro 9:1). 

streets--or most public places, not secretly.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.3.intro.text:
The study of truth commended. God must be feared, honored, and trusted, and filial submission, under chastisement, exhibited. The excellence of wisdom urged and illustrated by its place in the divine counsels. Piety enforced by a contrast of the destiny of the righteous and the wicked. (Pro. 3:1-35)

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.5.intro.text:
A warning against the seductive arts of wicked women, enforced by considering the advantages of chastity, and the miserable end of the wicked. (Pro. 5:1-23)

This connection of wisdom and understanding is frequent (Pro 2:2; Pro 3:7); the first denotes the use of wise means for wise ends; the other, the exercise of a proper discrimination in their discovery.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.5.4.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.5.4.excerpt: her end--literally, "her future," in sense of reward, what follows (compare Psa 37:37; Psa 73:17). Its nature is evinced by the use of figures, opposite those of Pro 5:3. The physical and moral suffering of the deluded profligate are notoriously terrible.

In Pro 5:16, fountains (in the plural) rather denote the produce o
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.5.15-16.text: By figures, in which well, cistern, and fountain [Pro 5:15, Pro 5:18] represent the wife, and rivers of waters [Pro 5:16] the children, men are exhorted to constancy and satisfaction in lawful conjugal enjoyments. This train of thought seems to
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.6.intro.text:
After admonitions against suretyship and sloth (compare Pro 6:6-8), the character and fate of the wicked generally are set forth, and the writer (Pro. 6:20-35) resumes the warnings against incontinence, pointing out its certain and terrible results. This train of thought seems to intimate the kindred of these vices. (Pro. 6:1-35)

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.8.intro.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.8.intro.excerpt: Contrasted with sensual allurements are the advantages of divine wisdom, which publicly invites men, offers the best principles of life, and the most valuable benefits resulting from receiving her counsels. Her relation to the divine plans and acts is introduced, as in Pro 3:19-2
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.8.intro.text:
Contrasted with sensual allurements are the advantages of divine wisdom, which publicly invites men, offers the best principles of life, and the most valuable benefits resulting from receiving her counsels. Her relation to the divine plans and acts is introduced, as in Pro 3:19-20, though more fully, to commend her desirableness for men, and the whole is closed by an assurance that those finding her find God's favor, and those neglecting ruin themselves. Many regard the passage as a description of the Son of God by the title, Wisdom, which the older Jews used (and by which He is called in Luk 11:49), as Joh 1:1, &c., describes Him by that of Logos, the Word. But the passage may be taken as a personification of wisdom: for, (1) Though described as with God, wisdom is not asserted to be God. (2) The use of personal attributes is equally consistent with a personification, as with the description of a real person. (3) The personal pronouns used accord with the gender (feminine) of wisdom constantly, and are never changed to that of the person meant, as sometimes occurs in a corresponding use of spirit, which is neuter in Greek, but to which masculine pronouns are often applied (Joh 16:14), when the acts of the Holy Spirit are described. (4) Such a personification is agreeable to the style of this book (compare Pro 1:20; Pro 3:16-17; Pro 4:8; Pro 6:20-22; Pro 9:1-4), whereas no prophetical or other allusions to the Saviour or the new dispensation are found among the quotations of this book in the New Testament, and unless this be such, none exist. (5) Nothing is lost as to the importance of this passage, which still remains a most ornate and also solemn and impressive teaching of inspiration on the value of wisdom. (Pro. 8:1-36)

The publicity and universality of the call contrast with the secrecy and intrigues of the wicked (Pro 7:8, &c.).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.8.22.text:

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.10.intro.text:
Here begins the second part of the book, Pro. 10:1-22:16, which, with the third, Pro. 22:16-25:28, contains series of proverbs whose sense is complete in one or two verses, and which, having no logical connection, admit of no analysis. The parallelisms of Pro. 10:1-15:33 are mostly antithetic; and those of Pro. 16:1-22:16, synthetic. The evidences of art in the structure are very clear, and indicate, probably, a purpose of facilitating the labor of memorizing. (Pro. 10:1-32)

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.31.excerpt: when . . . red--the color denoting greater strength (compare Gen 49:11; Deu 32:14). giveth . . . cup--literally, "gives its eye," that is, sparkles. moveth . . . aright--Perhaps its foaming is meant.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.32.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.32.excerpt: The acute miseries resulting from drunkenness contrasted with the temptations.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.32.text: The acute miseries resulting from drunkenness contrasted with the temptations.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.33-34.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.33-34.excerpt: The moral effects: it inflames passion (Gen 19:31, Gen 19:35), lays open the heart, produces insensibility to the greatest dangers, and debars from reformation, under the severest sufferings.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.35.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.23.35.excerpt: awake--that is, from drunkenness (Gen 9:24). This is the language rather of acts than of the tongue. Next: Proverbs Chapter 24

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.2.excerpt: studieth--meditateth. talk . . . mischief--Their expressed purposes are to do evil.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.5-6.excerpt: The general statement (Ecc 9:16, Ecc 9:18) is specially illustrated (compare Pro 21:22; Psa 144:1).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.8.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.8.excerpt: So called even if he fails to do evil.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.8.text: So called even if he fails to do evil.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.10.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.10.excerpt: Literally, "If thou fail in the day of straits (adversity), strait (or, small) is thy strength," which is then truly tested.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.10.text: Literally, "If thou fail in the day of straits (adversity), strait (or, small) is thy strength," which is then truly tested.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.11-12.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.11-12.excerpt: Neglect of known duty is sin (Jam 4:17). ready--literally, "bowing down" to be slain--that is, unjustly. God's retributive justice cannot be avoided by professed ignorance.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.11-12.text:
Neglect of known duty is sin (Jam 4:17). 

ready--literally, "bowing down" 

to be slain--that is, unjustly. God's retributive justice cannot be avoided by professed ignorance.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.13.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.13.excerpt: As delicious food whets the appetite, so should the rewards of wisdom excite us to seek it.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.13.text: As delicious food whets the appetite, so should the rewards of wisdom excite us to seek it.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.14.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.14.excerpt: reward--literally, "after part," the proper result (compare Pro 23:18; Psa 37:37-38).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.14.text: reward--literally, "after part," the proper result (compare Pro 23:18; Psa 37:37-38).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.15.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.15.excerpt: The plots of the wicked against the good, though partially, shall not be fully successful (Psa 37:24); while the wicked, falling under penal evil, find no help.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.15.text: The plots of the wicked against the good, though partially, shall not be fully successful (Psa 37:24); while the wicked, falling under penal evil, find no help.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.16.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.16.excerpt: seven times--often, or many (Pro 6:16, Pro 6:31; Pro 9:1).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.16.text: seven times--often, or many (Pro 6:16, Pro 6:31; Pro 9:1).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.17-18.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.17-18.excerpt: Yet let none rejoice over the fate of evildoers, lest God punish their wrong spirit by relieving the sufferer (compare Pro 17:5; Job 31:29).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.17-18.text: Yet let none rejoice over the fate of evildoers, lest God punish their wrong spirit by relieving the sufferer (compare Pro 17:5; Job 31:29).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.20.excerpt: candle--or, "prosperity"; it shall come to an end (Pro 13:9; Pro 20:20).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.20.text: candle--or, "prosperity"; it shall come to an end (Pro 13:9; Pro 20:20).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.21.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.21.excerpt: A warning against impiety and resistance to lawful rule (Rom 13:1-7; Pe1 2:17). meddle . . . change--(Compare Margin), literally, "mingle not yourself," avoid the society of restless persons.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.21.text:
A warning against impiety and resistance to lawful rule (Rom 13:1-7; Pe1 2:17). 

meddle . . . change--(Compare Margin), literally, "mingle not yourself," avoid the society of restless persons.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.22.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.22.excerpt: their calamity, &c.--either what God and the king inflict, or what changers and their company suffer; better the first.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.22.text: their calamity, &c.--either what God and the king inflict, or what changers and their company suffer; better the first.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.23.excerpt: These . . . wise--literally, "are of the wise," as authors (compare "Psalms of David," Hebrew). "These" refers to the verses following, Pro 24:24-34. to have respect--literally, "to discern faces," show partiality,

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.26.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.26.excerpt: kiss his lips--love and obey, do homage (Psa 2:12; Sol 8:1). right answer--literally, "plain words" (compare Pro 8:9), opposed to deceptive, or obscure.

kiss his lips--love and obey, do homage (Psa 2:12; Sol 8:1).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.27.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.27.excerpt: Prepare . . . in the field--Secure, by diligence, a proper support, and then build; provide necessaries, then comforts, to which a house rather pertained, in a mild climate, permitting the use of tents.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.28.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.28.excerpt: Do not speak even truth needlessly against any, and never falsehood.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.28.text: Do not speak even truth needlessly against any, and never falsehood.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.30-31.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.30-31.excerpt: A striking picture of the effects of sloth.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.30-31.text: A striking picture of the effects of sloth.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.32-34.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.32-34.excerpt: From the folly of the sluggard learn wisdom (Pro 6:10-11). Next: Proverbs Chapter 25
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.24.32-34.text:
From the folly of the sluggard learn wisdom (Pro 6:10-11).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.intro.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.intro.excerpt: (Pro. 25:1-28) The character of these proverbs sustains the title (see Introduction). also--refers to the former part of the book. copied out--literally, "transferred," that is, from some other book to this; not given from memory.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.2.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.2.excerpt: God's unsearchableness impresses us with awe (compare Isa 45:15; Rom 11:33). But kings, being finite, should confer with wise counsellors;
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.2.text: God's unsearchableness impresses us with awe (compare Isa 45:15; Rom 11:33). But kings, being finite, should confer with wise counsellors;

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.3.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.3.excerpt: Ye wisely keeping state secrets, which to common men are as inaccessible heights and depths.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.3.text: Ye wisely keeping state secrets, which to common men are as inaccessible heights and depths.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.4.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.4.excerpt: As separating impurities from ore leaves pure silver, so taking from a king wicked counsellors leaves a wise and beneficent government.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.4.text: As separating impurities from ore leaves pure silver, so taking from a king wicked counsellors leaves a wise and beneficent government.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.5.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.5.excerpt: before--or, "in presence of," as courtiers stood about a king.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.5.text: before--or, "in presence of," as courtiers stood about a king.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.6-7.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.6-7.excerpt: Do not intrude into the presence of the king, for the elevation of the humble is honorable, but the humbling of the proud disgraceful (Luk 14:8-10).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.6-7.text: Do not intrude into the presence of the king, for the elevation of the humble is honorable, but the humbling of the proud disgraceful (Luk 14:8-10).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.8.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.8.excerpt: (Compare Pro 3:30). lest . . . shame--lest you do what you ought not, when shamed by defeat, or "lest thou art shut out from doing any thing."
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.8.text:
(Compare Pro 3:30). 

lest . . . shame--lest you do what you ought not, when shamed by defeat, or "lest thou art shut out from doing any thing."

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.9-10.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.9-10.excerpt: (Compare Mat 5:25, Margin). secret--that is, of your opponent, for his disadvantage, and so you be disgraced, not having discussed your difficulties with him.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.9-10.text:
(Compare Mat 5:25, Margin). 

secret--that is, of your opponent, for his disadvantage, and so you be disgraced, not having discussed your difficulties with him.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.11.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.11.excerpt: a word fitly--literally, "quickly," as wheels roll, just in time. The comparison as apples . . . silver gives a like sense. apples, &c.--either real apples of golden color, in a silver network basket, or imitations on silver embroidery.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.11.text:
a word fitly--literally, "quickly," as wheels roll, just in time. The comparison as apples . . . silver gives a like sense. 

apples, &c.--either real apples of golden color, in a silver network basket, or imitations on silver embroidery.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.12.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.12.excerpt: Those who desire to know and do rightly, most highly esteem good counsel (Pro 9:9; Pro 15:31). The listening ear is better than one hung with gold.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.12.text: Those who desire to know and do rightly, most highly esteem good counsel (Pro 9:9; Pro 15:31). The listening ear is better than one hung with gold.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.13.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.13.excerpt: Snow from mountains was used to cool drinks; so refreshing is a faithful messenger (Pro 13:17).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.13.text: Snow from mountains was used to cool drinks; so refreshing is a faithful messenger (Pro 13:17).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.14.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.14.excerpt: clouds--literally, "vapors" (Jer 10:13), clouds only in appearance. a false gift--promised, but not given.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.14.text:
clouds--literally, "vapors" (Jer 10:13), clouds only in appearance. 

a false gift--promised, but not given.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.15.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.15.excerpt: Gentleness and kindness overcome the most powerful and obstinate. long forbearing--or, "slowness to anger" (Pro 14:29; Pro 15:18).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.15.text:
Gentleness and kindness overcome the most powerful and obstinate. 

long forbearing--or, "slowness to anger" (Pro 14:29; Pro 15:18).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.16-17.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.16-17.excerpt: A comparison, as a surfeit of honey produces physical disgust, so your company, however agreeable in moderation, may, if excessive, lead your friend to hate you.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.16-17.text: A comparison, as a surfeit of honey produces physical disgust, so your company, however agreeable in moderation, may, if excessive, lead your friend to hate you.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.18.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.18.excerpt: A false witness is as destructive to reputation, as such weapons to the body (Pro 24:28). beareth . . . witness--literally, "answereth questions," as before a judge, against his neighbor.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.18.text:
A false witness is as destructive to reputation, as such weapons to the body (Pro 24:28). 

beareth . . . witness--literally, "answereth questions," as before a judge, against his neighbor.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.19.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.19.excerpt: Treachery annoys as well as deceives.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.19.text: Treachery annoys as well as deceives.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.20.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.20.excerpt: Not only is the incongruity of songs (that is, joyful) and sadness meant, but an accession of sadness, by want of sympathy, is implied.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.20.text: Not only is the incongruity of songs (that is, joyful) and sadness meant, but an accession of sadness, by want of sympathy, is implied.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.21-22.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.21-22.excerpt: (Compare Mat 5:44; Rom 12:20). As metals are melted by heaping coals upon them, so is the heart softened by kindness.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.21-22.text: (Compare Mat 5:44; Rom 12:20). As metals are melted by heaping coals upon them, so is the heart softened by kindness.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.23.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.23.excerpt: Better, "As the north wind bringeth forth (Psa 90:2) or produces rain, so does a concealed or slandering tongue produce anger."
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.23.text: Better, "As the north wind bringeth forth (Psa 90:2) or produces rain, so does a concealed or slandering tongue produce anger."

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.25.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.25.excerpt: (Compare Pro 25:13). good news--that is, of some loved interest or absent friend, the more grateful as coming from afar.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.25.text:
(Compare Pro 25:13). 

good news--that is, of some loved interest or absent friend, the more grateful as coming from afar.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.26.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.26.excerpt: From troubled fountains and corrupt springs no healthy water is to be had, so when the righteous are oppressed by the wicked, their power for good is lessened or destroyed.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.26.text: From troubled fountains and corrupt springs no healthy water is to be had, so when the righteous are oppressed by the wicked, their power for good is lessened or destroyed.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.27.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.27.excerpt: Satiety surfeits (Pro 25:16); so men who are self-glorious find shame. is not glory--"not" is supplied from the first clause, or "is grievous," in which sense a similar word is used (Pro 27:2).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.27.text:
Satiety surfeits (Pro 25:16); so men who are self-glorious find shame. 

is not glory--"not" is supplied from the first clause, or "is grievous," in which sense a similar word is used (Pro 27:2).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.28.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.28.excerpt: Such are exposed to the incursions of evil thoughts and successful temptations. Next: Proverbs Chapter 26
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.25.28.text:
Such are exposed to the incursions of evil thoughts and successful temptations.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.intro.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.intro.excerpt: (Pro. 26:1-28) The incongruities of nature illustrate also those of the moral world. The fool's unworthiness is also implied (Pro 17:7; Pro 19:10).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.intro.text:
(Pro. 26:1-28)

The incongruities of nature illustrate also those of the moral world. The fool's unworthiness is also implied (Pro 17:7; Pro 19:10).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.2.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.2.excerpt: Though not obvious to us, the bird--literally, "sparrow"--and swallow--have an object in their motions, so penal evil falls on none without a reason.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.2.text:
Though not obvious to us, 

the bird--literally, "sparrow"--and 

swallow--have an object in their motions, so penal evil falls on none without a reason.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.3.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.3.excerpt: The rod is as much needed by fools and as well suited to them, as whips and bridles are for beasts.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.3.text: The rod is as much needed by fools and as well suited to them, as whips and bridles are for beasts.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.4.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.4.excerpt: Answer not--that is, approvingly by like folly.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.4.text: Answer not--that is, approvingly by like folly.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.6.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.6.excerpt: A fool fails by folly as surely as if he were maimed. drinketh damage--that is, gets it abundantly (Job 15:16; Job 34:7).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.6.text:
A fool fails by folly as surely as if he were maimed. 

drinketh damage--that is, gets it abundantly (Job 15:16; Job 34:7).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.7.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.7.excerpt: legs . . . equal--or, "take away the legs," or "the legs . . . are weak." In any case the idea is that they are the occasion of an awkwardness, such as the fool shows in using a parable or proverb (see Introduction; Pro 17:7).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.7.text: legs . . . equal--or, "take away the legs," or "the legs . . . are weak." In any case the idea is that they are the occasion of an awkwardness, such as the fool shows in using a parable or proverb (see Introduction; Pro 17:7).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.8.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.8.excerpt: A stone, bound in a sling, is useless; so honor, conferred on a fool, is thrown away.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.8.text: A stone, bound in a sling, is useless; so honor, conferred on a fool, is thrown away.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.9.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.9.excerpt: As vexatious and unmanageable as a thorn in a drunkard's hand is a parable to a fool. He will be as apt to misuse is as to use it rightly.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.9.text: As vexatious and unmanageable as a thorn in a drunkard's hand is a parable to a fool. He will be as apt to misuse is as to use it rightly.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.10.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.10.excerpt: Various versions of this are proposed (compare Margin). Better perhaps--"Much He injures (or literally, "wounds") all who reward," &c., that is, society is injured by encouraging evil men. transgressors--may be rendered "vagrants." The word "God" is improperly supplied.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.26.10.text:
Various versions of this are proposed (compare Margin). Better perhaps--"Much He injures (or literally, "wounds") all who reward," &c., that is, society is injured by encouraging evil men. 

transgressors--may be rendered "vagrants." The word "God" is improperly supplied.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.30.intro.excerpt: (Pro. 30:1-33) This is the title of this chapter (see Introduction). the prophecy--literally, "the burden" (compare Isa 13:1; Zac 9:1), used for any divine instruction; not necessarily a prediction, which was only a kind of prophecy (Ch1 15:27, "a song"). Prophets were inspire
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.30.intro.text:
(Pro. 30:1-33)

This is the title of this chapter (see Introduction). 

the prophecy--literally, "the burden" (compare Isa 13:1; Zac 9:1), used for any divine instruction; not necessarily a prediction, which was only a kind of prophecy (Ch1 15:27, "a song"). Prophets were inspired men, who spoke for God to man, or for man to God (Gen 20:7; Exo 7:14-16). Such, also, were the New Testament prophets. In a general sense, Gad, Nathan, and others were such, who were divine teachers, though we do not learn that they ever predicted. 

the man spake--literally, "the saying of the man"; an expression used to denote any solemn and important announcement (compare Sa2 23:1; Psa 36:1; Psa 110:1; Isa 1:24, &c.). Ithiel and Ucal were perhaps pupils.

The questions of this clause emphatically deny the attributes mentioned to be thos
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.30.2-4.text: brutish--stupid, a strong term to denote his lowly self-estimation; or he may speak of such as his natural condition, as contrasted with God's all-seeing comprehensive knowledge and almighty power. The questions of this clause emphatically deny the attributes mentioned to be those of any creature, thus impressively strengthening the implied reference of the former to God (compare Deu 30:12-14; Isa 40:12; Eph 4:8).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.30.24-25.text: These verses provide two classes of apt illustrations of various aspects of the moral world, which the reader is left to apply. By the first (Pro 30:25-28), diligence and providence are commended; the success of these insignificant animals being due to their instinctive sagacity and activity, rather than strength. The other class (Pro 30:30-31) provides similes for whatever is majestic or comely, uniting efficiency with gracefulness.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.15.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.15.excerpt: She diligently attends to expending as well as gathering wealth;
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.15.text: She diligently attends to expending as well as gathering wealth;

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.16.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.16.excerpt: and hence has means to purchase property.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.16.text: and hence has means to purchase property.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.17-18.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.17-18.excerpt: To energy she adds a watchfulness in bargains, and a protracted and painful industry. The last clause may figuratively denote that her prosperity (compare Pro 24:20) is not short lived.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.17-18.text: To energy she adds a watchfulness in bargains, and a protracted and painful industry. The last clause may figuratively denote that her prosperity (compare Pro 24:20) is not short lived.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.19.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.19.excerpt: No work, however mean, if honest, is disdained.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.19.text: No work, however mean, if honest, is disdained.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.20.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.20.excerpt: Industry enables her to be charitable.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.20.text: Industry enables her to be charitable.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.21.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.21.excerpt: scarlet--or, "purple," by reason of the dyes used, the best fabrics; as a matter of taste also; the color suits cold.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.21.text: scarlet--or, "purple," by reason of the dyes used, the best fabrics; as a matter of taste also; the color suits cold.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.22.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.22.excerpt: coverings of tapestry--or, "coverlets," that is, for beds. silk--or, "linen" (compare Exo 26:1; Exo 27:9) and purple--that is, the most costly goods.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.22.text:
coverings of tapestry--or, "coverlets," that is, for beds. 

silk--or, "linen" (compare Exo 26:1; Exo 27:9) 

and purple--that is, the most costly goods.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.23.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.23.excerpt: in the gates--(compare Pro 22:22). His domestic comfort promotes his advancement in public dignity.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.23.text: in the gates--(compare Pro 22:22). His domestic comfort promotes his advancement in public dignity.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.24.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.24.excerpt: fine linen--or, "linen shirts," or the material for them. girdles--were often costly and highly valued (Sa2 18:11). delivereth--or, "giveth as a present" or "to sell."
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.24.text:
fine linen--or, "linen shirts," or the material for them. 

girdles--were often costly and highly valued (Sa2 18:11). 

delivereth--or, "giveth as a present" or "to sell."

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.25.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.25.excerpt: Strength and honour--Strong and beautiful is her clothing; or, figuratively, for moral character, vigorous and honorable. shall rejoice . . . come--in confidence of certain maintenance.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.25.text:
Strength and honour--Strong and beautiful is her clothing; or, figuratively, for moral character, vigorous and honorable. 

shall rejoice . . . come--in confidence of certain maintenance.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.26.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.26.excerpt: Her conversation is wise and gentle.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.26.text: Her conversation is wise and gentle.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.27.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.27.excerpt: (Compare Ti1 5:14; Tit 2:5). She adds to her example a wise management of those under her control.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.27.text: (Compare Ti1 5:14; Tit 2:5). She adds to her example a wise management of those under her control.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.28.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.28.excerpt: She is honored by those who best know her.
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.28.text: She is honored by those who best know her.

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.29.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.29.excerpt: The words are those of her husband, praising her. virtuously--(Compare Pro 31:10).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.29.text:
The words are those of her husband, praising her. 

virtuously--(Compare Pro 31:10).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.30.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.30.excerpt: Favour--or, "Grace" of personal manner. beauty--of face, or form (compare Pro 11:22). True piety alone commands permanent respect and affection (Pe1 3:3).
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.30.text:
Favour--or, "Grace" of personal manner. 

beauty--of face, or form (compare Pro 11:22). True piety alone commands permanent respect and affection (Pe1 3:3).

jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.31.author: Jamieson, Fausset & Brown
jamieson-fausset-brown.Prov.31.31.excerpt: The result of her labor is her best eulogy. Nothing can add to the simple beauty of this admirable portrait. On the measure of its realization in the daughters of our own day rest untold results, in the domestic, and, therefore, the civil and religious, welfare of the people.
